quotes.quote: We introduce the AI Productivity Index for Software Engineering (APEX–SWE), a benchmark for assessing whether frontier AI models can execute economically valuable software engineering work.
We evaluated eleven frontier models for the APEX–SWE leaderboard.
We open-source the APEX–SWE evaluation harness and a dev set (n = 50).

APEX–SWE assesses two novel task types that reflect real-world software engineering: (1) Integration tasks (n = 100), which require constructing end-to-end systems across heterogeneous cloud primitives, business applications, and infrastructure-as-code services, and (2) Observability tasks (n = 100), which require debugging production failures using telemetry signals such as logs and dashboards, as well as unstructured context.
Our analysis shows that strong performance is primarily driven by epistemic discipline, defined as the capacity to distinguish between assumptions and verified facts.

Yet industry data shows a fundamental mismatch between what existing benchmarks measure and what professional software engineers do: according to IDC, developers spend only 16% of their time writing application code (Resnick, 2025).

The benchmark has become saturated – frontier models cluster around 80% Pass@1, and OpenAI has declared the benchmark “contaminated” as models can reproduce original patches verbatim from task IDs alone (Glaese and Watkins, 2026).
Models interact with the environment through a ReAct harness, which works in a persistent, multistep loop.
It iterates until it outputs a <task_complete> tag or reaches the wall-clock timeout of one hour.

Models have access to three categories of tools: (1) Terminal (Bash execution via /bin/bash in a persistent tmux session), (2) File Operations (with read/write access to the workspace), and (3) Model Context Protocol (MCP) Servers (i.e., API access to services such as Loki, Plane, Medusa).
We assess models’ outputs using Pass@1, defined as the average pass rate across three independent epochs (or “runs”).
We also report Pass@3, assessing if the model can achieve the correct outcome at least once over three epochs.
For Integration, correctness is verified via a pytest suite that interacts directly with service APIs.
Tasks were created by software engineers with 3+ years of experience.
Each case underwent a three-stage validation process.
Third, creation of a gold standard output to ensure that the human-authored solution passes all tests with a 100% score.
The tasks are derived from real-world GitHub Issue – PR pairs, sourced from repositories with at least 350 stars.
We filtered for complexity, selecting only patches with at least 100 lines of code impacting at least three files.

All Integration tasks include an ephemeral PostgreSQL database and Plane, as well as six other services: LocalStack (56%), which emulates AWS primitives (such as S3, Lambda, DynamoDB, and Kinesis), EspoCRM (35%), MailHog (33%) for SMTP testing, Mattermost (32%), Medusa (31%) for e-commerce, and Zammad (26%).

Each task deploys a containerized environment orchestrating five services: a client workspace, Loki and Promtail for log aggregation, Grafana for visualization, and Plane/Mattermost for ticket and chat context.
Observability tasks are across five languages: Go (30%), Python (25%), TypeScript (25%), Java (10%), and C++ (10%).

The model is provided with a summary of the user issue, an interface.md file describing relevant repository functions, and specifications for available Model Context Protocol (MCP) (Anthropic, 2024) tools.
Beyond Pass@1, APEX–SWE evaluates engineering quality through rubrics.
We define three rubric categories.
They are each graded independently by an LM judge (Gemini 3 Pro, Temperature 0.1, Thinking=High).
Rubric scores are not used for the APEX–SWE leaderboard, which relies exclusively on Pass@1.
Claude Opus 4.6 leads the APEX–SWE leaderboard with 40.5% Pass@1, followed by Claude Opus 4.5 at 38.7%.
Claude Opus 4.5 leads in single-shot performance with 50.7% Pass@1, followed by Claude Opus 4.6 at 49.3%, Claude Sonnet 4.5 at 43.3%, and Cognition SWE-1.6 Preview at 42.3%.
Claude Opus 4.6 leads at 31.7% Pass@1, followed by Claude Opus 4.5 at 26.7% and GPT–5.2 Codex at 21.3%.
Tasks involving only one service (n = 53) achieve 39.5% mean Pass@1, while tasks requiring two or more services (n = 47) drop to 18.6% – a 20.9 percentage point gap.
Insufficient Verification accounts for 52% of failures, followed by Bad Environment Understanding (22%), Specification NonCompliance (14%), and Execution Failure (12%).
For instance, on Integration tasks, Kimi K2 Instruct achieves 75.0% rubric quality on Integration tasks despite only 18.3% Pass@1 – a 56.7 percentage point gap.
Grok 4 achieves 36.3% Pass@1 on Integration but only 46.4% Robustness – the lowest among models with comparable correctness.
All models are called via LiteLLM with retry logic (exponential backoff) and a maximum of three attempts per request.
Second, absolute scores are uniformly higher on the open-source set, averaging 40.7% compared to 27.9% on the leaderboard – an inflation of 12.8 percentage points.
The leaderboard comprises 100 Integration and 100 Observability tasks; the open-source set contains 25 of each.
Table 6 presents Pass@1 scores – averaging Integration and Observability performance – for each model on both sets.

The AI Productivity Index for Software Engineers (APEX-SWE) measures whether frontier AI systems can execute economically valuable software engineering work.

It comprises n=200 cases and spans two complementary settings that mirror professional SWE work: (1) Integration tasks that require end-to-end system construction and deployment across heterogeneous services and (2) Observability tasks that require debugging with production-style telemetry.
Each task includes a human-authored rubric that grades agent outputs for functional requirements, robustness, and code style, alongside unit tests.
Pass@1 measures the percentage of tasks that an agent successfully completes on a single attempt (i.e., scores 100% on the rubric).
Model outputs are graded using expert-authored rubrics with an LM judge.
The full task set stays private so that models can't be trained on it.
To support open research, we have open-sourced n=50 cases that are in-distribution of APEX-SWE on Hugging Face with all metadata labels.
Practicing professional software engineers from Mercor’s network of 5M+ experts.
It was developed in collaboration with Cognition.
Rankings can change whenever a frontier model is released.
New models are evaluated on APEX-Agents, APEX-SWE, APEX-Accounting and APEX-1 when they ship.

It measures whether frontier AI models can handle real software engineering work – shipping systems, diagnosing failures, and implementing fixes.
The remaining 84% involves CI/CD, infrastructure monitoring, deployment, and debugging.
GPT-4 has improved from 67% to 90% on HumanEval in just two years, and the most recent Opus models consistently score over 75% on SWE-bench Verified.
At the time of release, the top score on the APEX-SWE leaderboard is GPT-5.3 Codex at 41.5% Pass@1, leaving plenty of room for hillclimbing.
GPT-5.3 Codex (High) tops the leaderboard at 41.5%, followed by Opus 4.6 (High) at 40.5% on Pass@1 and Opus 4.6 (High) at 38.7%.
For Integration, Claude Opus 4.5 (High) and GPT 5.4 (High) lead at 50.7%.
Observability scores are lower overall, with GPT 5.3 Codex leading at 33.3% Pass@1.
Models perform better on Integration tasks than Observability tasks.
Tasks were created by software engineers with 3+ years of experience who ran validation tests and created gold standard outputs.

They all include an ephemeral PostgreSQL database and Plane, as well as six other services: LocalStack (56%), which emulates AWS primitives such as S3, Lambda, DynamoDB, and Kinesis, EspoCRM (35%), MailHog (33%), Mattermost (32%), Medusa (31%), and Zammad (26%).

Engineers scripted synthetic logs (500 to 1,000 lines of normal operation mixed with 10-20 lines of bug symptoms) and chat history to replicate a production failure, as well as Dockerfiles, task metadata, and patches.
Tasks were derived from real-world GitHub Issue-PR pairs, sourced from repositories with at least 350 stars that we filtered for complexity and stability.
Observability tasks are distributed across five widely-used languages: Go (30%), Python (25%), TypeScript (25%), Java (10%), and C++ (10%).
We have released an open-source dev set via Hugging Face (n=50) with a CC-BY license, and our eval harness is available as an open-source repo on GitHub.
The full leaderboard comprises n=200 tasks that are heldout and hidden, with a similar distribution to the open-source set.
